sections.section_title: Introduction to Phase Change from Time Shifting
sections.learning_goal: Teach the time-shift phase rule for complex Fourier series coefficients and show that the magnitude stays fixed while the phase changes by $-k\omega_0 t_0$.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the time-shift rule for $x(t-t_0)$ in complex Fourier series form and connect it to a phase subtraction of $k\omega_0 t_0$ for each harmonic.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one coefficient $c_k = |c_k|e^{j\phi_k}$ and a positive shift $t_0$, then show that the shifted coefficient keeps $|c_k|$ and becomes $|c_k|e^{j(\phi_k-k\omega_0 t_0)}$.
paragraph_plan: Open with the coefficient-level time-shift property and name the exact change: phase shifts, magnitude stays fixed.
Rewrite a generic coefficient in polar form so the phase update is visible.
Show the phase subtraction $\phi'_k = \phi_k - k\omega_0 t_0$ and note that the shift scales with the harmonic index $k$.
Call out the $k=0$ special case and explain why the DC term does not rotate.
Close with a compact summary that the rule is symbolic, reusable, and avoids recomputing Fourier integrals.

sections.handoff_notes: Direct instruction only; keep the tutorial symbolic, concise, and focused on the general phase subtraction rule with no practice questions and no images.

sections.section_title: Phase Update for One Shifted Fourier Coefficient
sections.learning_goal: Apply the phase subtraction rule to one Fourier coefficient and write the shifted coefficient in polar form.

question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the shifted coefficient $c'_2$ after shifting $x(t)$ to $x(t-T_0/4)$ when the original coefficient is $c_2 = 4e^{j\pi/6}$?
distractor_plan: Add the shift angle instead of subtracting it.
Omit the factor of $k$ and use only $\omega_0 t_0$.
Change the magnitude instead of only the phase.
Keep the original phase unchanged.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $c_2 = 4e^{j\pi/6}$ for a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$, find the new $k=2$ coefficient of $x(t-T_0/4)$ in polar form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute the single-harmonic phase change, subtract it from the original phase, and preserve the magnitude.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from the general rule to one concrete nonzero harmonic with a specific shift.
solution_step_plan: Write the coefficient in polar form and identify the harmonic index $k=2$.
Compute the phase change $k\omega_0 t_0$ for $t_0=T_0/4$.
Subtract that angle from the original phase $\pi/6$.
Rewrite the new coefficient with the same magnitude and the updated phase.
practice_variation_axes: Change the harmonic index while keeping the same shift fraction.
Change the original coefficient phase from a positive angle to a negative angle.
Ask for the new phase only instead of the full coefficient.
Use a different simple fraction of $T_0$ so the phase subtraction stays clean.

sections.handoff_notes: Use a single concrete coefficient, keep the work symbolic-only, and build the practice set as five-choice multiple-choice items that test phase subtraction versus common sign and magnitude errors.

sections.section_title: Phase Updates Across Multiple Harmonic Indices
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same phase subtraction rule across several harmonics and show that the DC term stays fixed while each nonzero harmonic gets a different phase change.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text-only choices listing the updated phases for several harmonics.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which set of shifted phases is correct for $c_0 = 3$, $c_1 = 2e^{j\pi/3}$, and $c_3 = e^{-j\pi/2}$ after shifting by $x(t-T_0/6)$?
distractor_plan: Treat every harmonic as if it received the same phase shift.
Shift the DC term even though $k=0$.
Use the correct common angle but multiply by the wrong harmonic index.
Flip the sign of the phase change for one or more harmonics.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has $c_0 = 3$, $c_1 = 2e^{j\pi/3}$, and $c_3 = e^{-j\pi/2}$. Find the shifted phases for $x(t-T_0/6)$ and write the new coefficient phases for $k=0,1,3$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Apply the same phase subtraction rule to several harmonics and show that the DC term stays fixed while each nonzero harmonic gets a different phase change.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extend the one-coefficient update to a short coefficient list and include the $k=0$ term.
solution_step_plan: Compute the common shift angle $\omega_0 t_0$ once for $t_0=T_0/6$.
Multiply that angle by each harmonic index $k$ in the list.
Update $\phi'_0$, $\phi'_1$, and $\phi'_3$ one by one.
Check that the $k=0$ term does not change.
Summarize the phase ramp across the spectrum.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of harmonics in the list.
Include a coefficient with a negative phase angle.
Vary $t_0$ so the common shift angle changes.
Ask for the whole updated phase set instead of a single coefficient.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example as a short coefficient list, keep the spectrum symbolic-only, and make the practice set distinguish harmonic-dependent phase shifts from a uniform offset.

sections.section_title: Phase Sign for Delays and Advances
sections.learning_goal: Use the sign of $t_0$ to distinguish delay from advance and determine whether the phase increases or decreases.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text-only choices comparing the delay and advance phase changes or giving the shifted coefficient.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which statement correctly compares the phase change for a delay $x(t-T_0/8)$ and an advance $x(t+T_0/8)$ at harmonic $k=1$?
distractor_plan: Treat an advance as a delay.
Use $|t_0|$ instead of the signed shift.
Add the phase change when subtraction is required.
Ignore the harmonic index when comparing the two shifts.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the coefficient $c_1 = 5e^{-j\pi/4}$, compare the new phase for $x(t-T_0/8)$ with the new phase for $x(t+T_0/8)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the sign of $t_0$ to distinguish delay from advance and determine whether the phase increases or decreases.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keep one coefficient but flip the sign of the time shift so the learner sees the delay/advance contrast.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite $x(t+T_0/8)$ as a negative shift.
Compute $\omega_0 t_0$ for $T_0/8$ and apply the subtraction rule.
Compare the phase updates for the positive and negative shifts.
State the sign rule in words: delays subtract phase and advances add phase.
practice_variation_axes: Change the harmonic index from $k=1$ to another value.
Change the shift fraction while keeping the delay/advance contrast.
Ask for the sign of the phase change instead of the full coefficient.
Use a coefficient with a different starting phase so the arithmetic is not copied.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the contrast between positive and negative shifts explicit, use the same symbolic rule in both cases, and make the distractors target sign mistakes rather than algebraic complexity.

sections.section_title: Reading the Shifted Phase Spectrum

question_policy.answer_format: Five text-only choices that list a phase spectrum or describe the shift pattern.

Choose a spectrum with the wrong linear slope in $k$.
Flip the sign of the phase ramp.
Shift only the DC term instead of the whole spectrum.

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Interpret a shifted phase spectrum, recognize the linear ramp, and infer the shift size from the per-harmonic phase decrement.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from computing individual phase updates to reading the completed spectrum as a pattern.
solution_step_plan: Read the shifted phases and note that magnitudes are unchanged.
Compare the phase difference between adjacent harmonics.
Recognize the constant step size as $-\omega_0 t_0$.
Match the table to the time shift and state the phase-ramp pattern.
practice_variation_axes: Change the phase-ramp slope while keeping the spectrum linear in $k$.
Include a nonzero starting phase for the $k=0$ term.
Vary the number of harmonic indices shown in the spectrum.
Ask for the matching shift value or the matching spectrum description.

sections.handoff_notes: Treat this as the reading-and-recognition step: keep the spectrum symbolic-only, emphasize the linear phase ramp, and make the multiple-choice options distinguish a true $k$-dependent ramp from uniform or sign-flipped alternatives.

sections.learning_goal: Teach that a time shift changes each Fourier coefficient by the factor $c_k' = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ and that this factor has unit magnitude, so $|c_k'| = |c_k|$.

Confuse magnitude symmetry with phase symmetry.
Copy the coefficient values rather than taking absolute values.
Give a magnitude pair that is numerically inconsistent with $c_1$.

solution_step_plan: Compute the magnitude of the positive-harmonic coefficient.
Reuse that same value for the negative-harmonic coefficient.
State the even-magnitude symmetry across $\pm k$.

sections.section_title: Finding Odd Phase Symmetry
sections.learning_goal: Use conjugate symmetry to read odd phase symmetry directly from the coefficient pair.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the phase symmetry can be handled symbolically.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices with one correct phase pair or phase-symmetry statement.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $c_2 = 1 + j$, which choice gives the phase at $k=-2$ when the phase at $k=2$ is $45$ degrees?
distractor_plan: Keep the phase sign unchanged.
Use the magnitude instead of the phase.
Negate the magnitude instead of the phase.
Use a phase value from the wrong harmonic index.
Mix the phase answer with a conjugated rectangular coefficient instead of a phase statement.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A real periodic signal has $c_2 = 1 + j$. If the phase of $c_2$ is $45$ degrees, what is the phase of $c_{-2}$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert the positive-harmonic phase to the negative-harmonic phase by flipping the sign and state that phase is odd in $k$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The wrinkle is that the coefficients are now read through their angles rather than their rectangular components.
solution_step_plan: Read or compute the phase of the positive-harmonic coefficient.
Negate that phase for the negative-harmonic coefficient.
Pair the phase result with the unchanged magnitude as a check.
Name the odd-phase symmetry across $\pm k$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the harmonic index.
Present the coefficient in rectangular or polar form.
Use a symmetry statement instead of a direct phase value.
Ask for the negative-harmonic phase with a simple degree or radian value.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sign flip the entire point of the example. Keep the magnitude visible only as a consistency check so the learner does not confuse the two symmetries.

sections.section_title: Using Conjugate Symmetry to Complete a Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Combine conjugate symmetry, even magnitude, and odd phase to complete a partial spectrum without recalculating any integrals.

Use one correct conjugate pair and one pair with a sign error.

Swap the magnitude and phase symmetry statements.
Complete only part of the spectrum and leave one mirrored pair inconsistent.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A real periodic signal has $c_0 = 2$, $c_1 = 1 - j$, and $c_2 = -2j$. Complete the missing negative-harmonic coefficients and state the matching magnitude and phase symmetry.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine conjugate symmetry, even magnitude, and odd phase to complete a partial spectrum without recalculating any integrals.

solution_step_plan: Mirror each given positive-harmonic coefficient to its negative index.
Keep $c_0$ real.
Derive the magnitude symmetry from the conjugate pairs.
Derive the phase sign flip from the conjugate pairs.
Verify that the completed spectrum is internally consistent.
practice_variation_axes: Mix rectangular and polar coefficient forms.
Leave different subsets of the negative side blank.
Ask for a completed coefficient table or a symmetry summary.
Vary the harmonic indices and keep the DC term as a check.

sections.handoff_notes: End with a full spectrum completion so the learner practices the rule, the magnitude symmetry, and the phase symmetry together. Keep the task symbolic and table-based.

entries.lesson_core_move: Select and apply the appropriate Fourier series property to convert known coefficients into coefficients for a shifted, scaled, reversed, vertically shifted, or real-signal variant without recomputing the coefficient integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.learning_goal: Teach the learner to inspect a transformed periodic signal with known $c_k$, match it to the right Fourier series property or property chain, and update coefficients directly instead of re-integrating.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the task is to recognize the transformation on a periodic signal with known coefficients and reuse the matching property or property composition.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A single known signal $x(t)$ with coefficients $c_k$ is changed by one simple transformation such as $x(t-t_0)$ or $x(t)+A$.
paragraph_plan: Open with the lesson-level payoff: the learner already knows the property formulas, so the job is to recognize the transformation and reuse the right one.
List the cues to scan for in the signal statement: time shift, time scaling, time reversal, vertical offset, and real-signal symmetry.
Show how one property updates the coefficient rule and how two properties can be chained when the signal has two transformations.
Close with a compact decision checklist for what changes in $c_k$, what changes only in $c_0$, and when negative indices are filled by symmetry.

sections.section_title: Selecting the Property from a Transformed Signal
sections.learning_goal: Given a transformed periodic signal, choose the correct Fourier-series property or property combination before doing any coefficient arithmetic.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct property or property-combination rule.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)$ with coefficients $c_k$, identify the correct property for $y(t)=x(-t)$ and the matching coefficient-index rule.
distractor_plan: Use a time-shift phase factor instead of index reversal.
Use a vertical-shift rule that changes only $c_0$.
Use a time-scaling rule that changes the period but not the index mapping.
Use conjugate symmetry without reversing the harmonic index.
Leave the coefficients unchanged.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has known coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(-t)$. Decide which Fourier-series property applies and state how the coefficient indices change.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize time reversal as an index swap in the coefficient sequence without any re-integration.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example stops at property selection and index mapping; it does not layer in an additional shift or scaling.
solution_step_plan: Read the transformation as time reversal.
Match it to the property that swaps harmonic indices.
State the coefficient update in the original index notation.
Check that no other transformation is present.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the transformed signal between $x(-t)$ and another reversal-based form such as $x(-t)+A$.
Ask for either the property name or the coefficient rule.
Vary which harmonic index is queried so the learner must map $k$ to $-k$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example diagnostic: the first job is to recognize the transformation, then state the matching coefficient rule.

sections.section_title: Updating Known Coefficients with One Fourier Series Property
sections.learning_goal: Apply one Fourier-series property directly to update every coefficient in a transformed signal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct coefficient update rule.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$ and known coefficients $c_k$, choose the correct coefficient formula for the transformed signal.
distractor_plan: Leave the coefficients unchanged.
Use the wrong sign in the phase factor $e^{\pm jk\omega_0 t_0}$.
Apply the phase factor only to $c_0$ instead of every coefficient.
Replace the phase factor with a magnitude-only change.
Confuse the update with a time-reversal index swap.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. Find the coefficients of $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Apply the time-shift property to multiply each coefficient by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ while leaving the magnitudes unchanged.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example turns the selected property into a full coefficient update.
solution_step_plan: Identify the fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$ for the known signal.
Write the time-shift coefficient rule.
Multiply each $c_k$ by the phase factor $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$.
State that no coefficient magnitudes change and no integral is recomputed.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the sign of the shift to force the phase factor to flip sign.
Ask for a specific harmonic coefficient as well as the generic rule.
Vary the numerical value of $t_0$ while keeping the same update structure.

sections.handoff_notes: Show the update in compact coefficient notation; do not drift into a proof or a re-derivation of the property.

sections.section_title: Combining a Time Shift with a Vertical Shift
sections.learning_goal: Chain a time-shift update with a DC adjustment so the learner can handle a two-property coefficient transformation.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct combined coefficient update.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $y(t)=x(t+t_0)-A$, choose the correct updated Fourier coefficient rule.
distractor_plan: Add $A$ to every coefficient instead of only $c_0$.
Use the wrong sign in the time-shift phase factor.
Forget the phase factor entirely and only adjust the DC term.
Reverse the harmonic indices instead of shifting them.
Treat the offset as changing magnitudes rather than the DC coefficient.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. Find the coefficients of $y(t)=x(t-t_0)+A$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Apply the time-shift phase factor to every coefficient and then add $A$ only to $c_0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds a second independent transformation after the single-property update.
solution_step_plan: Apply the time-shift phase factor to every harmonic.
Adjust only the DC coefficient by adding $A$.
Leave every nonzero harmonic unchanged by the vertical shift.
Write the final coefficient sequence compactly.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the sign of $A$.
Vary whether the shift is a delay or an advance.
Ask for either the full coefficient list or just the DC term and one nonzero harmonic.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the two property updates ordered and explicit: shift first, then DC adjustment.

sections.section_title: Combining Time Reversal with Time Scaling
sections.learning_goal: Handle negative time scaling by tracking both the period change and the harmonic-index reversal in the coefficient update.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct period-and-coefficient rule.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $y(t)=x(-t/3)$ and known coefficients $c_k$, choose the correct new period and coefficient relation.
distractor_plan: Keep the old period unchanged.
Invert the scale factor incorrectly.
Apply only time reversal without changing the period.
Apply only scaling without reversing harmonic indices.
Confuse the update with a time-shift phase rule.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$ and period $T$. Determine the coefficients and new fundamental period of $y(t)=x(-2t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Track how negative time scaling changes the period and reverses the harmonic index while preserving the coefficient sequence under the scaling rule.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example combines reversal and scaling instead of using only one property.
solution_step_plan: Recognize that a negative scale factor combines time reversal with scaling.
Update the period and fundamental angular frequency.
Map each coefficient to the reversed harmonic index.
State the transformed coefficient sequence in the new indexing convention.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the negative scale factor.
Ask for either the new period, the new $\omega_0$, or the coefficient mapping.
Vary the signal so the learner must decide whether the negative sign triggers the reversal.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the two consequences of negative scaling explicit: the period changes, and the harmonic index order flips.

sections.section_title: Using Conjugate Symmetry to Complete Coefficient Updates
sections.learning_goal: Use conjugate symmetry to fill in the missing negative-harmonic coefficients after a property update on a real periodic signal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct completed coefficient set.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given the positive-harmonic coefficients of a real periodic signal after a transformation, choose the missing negative-harmonic coefficients that complete the sequence.
distractor_plan: Copy the positive coefficients without conjugating them.
Swap the conjugation direction.
Mix up the harmonic index sign.
Use a time-shift phase factor instead of symmetry.
Alter the DC coefficient even though it should remain real.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A real periodic signal has updated positive-harmonic coefficients after a transformation. Use conjugate symmetry to determine the missing negative-index coefficients and complete the spectrum.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use $d_{-k}=d_k^*$ for a real signal to fill the negative-harmonic coefficients after the update.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This closes the lesson by using symmetry to finish a partially updated coefficient set rather than recomputing anything.
solution_step_plan: Confirm that the signal is real.
Apply conjugate symmetry to each known positive-harmonic coefficient.
Compute the matching negative-harmonic coefficients.
Check that the DC coefficient remains real.
Present the completed spectrum.
practice_variation_axes: Vary which harmonics are missing.
Vary whether the known positive coefficients are purely real or fully complex.
Ask for the full completed sequence or only the negative-index entries.

sections.handoff_notes: Use symmetry to complete the update, not to introduce a new property; the learner should finish from the real-signal condition.
